title: P99/Tail Latency Deep Dive - Montara Analytics
summary: Technical deep dive focused on tail latency behavior under streaming and non-streaming modes. Discussed KV cache impacts, batching, quantization, and network hops for VPC/on-prem deployments. Agreed to run benchmarks with Montara traffic profile and follow up with security docs and pricing.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-03 15:30 PST
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Lara Bennett (Montara - Head of ML), Marco Ruiz (Infra Lead), Sofia Kim (CTO)

Summary: see above
Topics: p99/p95 tail, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache, batching, quantization, VPC hops

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda - run through p95/p99 numbers we've seen, dive into KV cache and batching, then mapping to your VPC topology and on prem constraints. priya will take the deep perf bits
[00:18] Lara: thanks alex, quick context — we're running a mix of chat and single-shot generation for our search assistant. typical length 60-180 tokens per call. SLA target for UX is p95 < 250ms, p99 < 600ms end-to-end if possible
[00:34] Priya: okay great, and is that streaming responses or do you render after full generation
[00:38] Lara: streaming ideally for chat, single-shot for some analytics endpoints. we saw p99 spikes in chat during peak which is why we wanted this deep dive
[00:52] Marco: fwiw our infra sits in a multi-AZ VPC, we use NLB to reach pods, and we have an on-prem fallback via direct connect. curious how much of the p99 is network vs runtime
[01:10] Priya: good question — we usually break E2E into three buckets: network hops (client -> LB -> router -> pod), model runtime (token gen + KV cache ops), and queuing/batching. in our instrumentation we tag the request at the edge and at the runtime to measue those regions
[01:28] Alex: i'll share our latency deck and a sample benchmark sheet after — link in chat: /links/redwood-latency-deck.pdf
[01:36] Marco: ok
[01:40] Priya: to give concrete numbers from a hosted cluster: for a 3B-ish model with streaming enabled, typical mean token latency is ~30ms, p95 token latency ~120ms, p99 ~320-420ms depending on sequence length and cache hit rate. non-streaming (batching) for full generation end-to-end p95 was ~180ms p99 ~500ms for a 100-200 token response in our tests
[02:05] Lara: that's interesting. are those numbers server-side only? what's typical network overhead
[02:11] Priya: yes server-side. network can add anywhere from 20ms (same AZ) to 120-200ms if cross-AZ or via on-prem hop, and TLS handshake/cold connections add more. so if you're cross region or hitting on-prem via DX, p99 can blow past 600ms easily
[02:30] Marco: how much does the KV cache change that? we rely on prefix caching a lot
[02:35] Priya: KV cache reduces token compute significantly on continuing sessions — our measurements show cache hits save 40-70% of runtime per token depending on attention cache reuse. but cache introduces variability: miss patterns cause spikes. also cache synchronization across replicas can add small consistency delays if you have multi-zone replication
[02:58] Speaker 1 (Sofia?): so for multi-AZ we should expect extra round trips for cache synchrony?
[03:04] Priya: depends on your deployment. if cache is local to the serving pod it's fast but you lose cross-replica hits; if you use a shared cache tier you add network latency. tradeoffs. for most real-time apps we recommend local KV with sticky routing so requests hit the pod with hot cache
[03:25] Marco: sticky session routing with NLB is doable but what about autoscaling / pod churn
[03:30] Priya: autoscaling churn is a challenge — you can warm caches via TTLs and background prefetch, and use request routing policies: route warm sessions to dedicated capacity or scale with grace periods. Redwood Dedicate lets you pin warm instances for high-frequency users
[03:46] Lara: can you explain batching impact for p99? we thought batching would always help latency
[03:51] Priya: simple answer: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency in some workloads. with continuous batching small micro-batches for low concurrency give you better per-request latency. large batching benefits throughput (cost) but you add queueing delay that inflates p99. We tune batch windows and adaptive thresholds based on arrival patterns
[04:17] Alex: quick interruption, sry — on quantization: what's the impact of int8 / 4-bit on latency vs quality
[04:24] Priya: quantization reduces per-token compute and memory bandwidth so server-side token latency drops — we see 20-40% lower token latency switching from fp16 to int8 or 4-bit quantized kernels. but quality delta depends on model and method; some models degrade more. we run A/B evals with your prompt sets to estimate quality loss. also quantized kernels sometimes have different p99 characteristics if fallback to slower kernels occurs for certain op patterns
[04:52] Lara: do you have notes on which quant configs you recommend for chat vs single-shot
[04:57] Priya: for chat we often use q4_k_m type profiles (4-bit with tuned per-channel scales) for a good latency/quality tradeoff. for high-accuracy analytics endpoints we stay fp16 or int8 with tuned calibration
[05:12] Marco: network hops question — in our topology we have client -> public ALB -> NLB -> k8s ingress -> service -> pod -> gpu. which of those are typical hotspots
[05:23] Priya: ALB/NLB + cross-AZ hops are common hotspots. k8s ingress adds small CPU latency, and serialization on the proxy can add jitter. GPU queuing and model load/unload are big causes if you don't keep warm instances. also TLS termination choices matter — terminating at the ALB vs at the pod impacts latency differently
[05:45] Sofia: we're considering on-prem for data residency. how different will tail latency be vs hosted
[05:50] Priya: on-prem can be better if you place clients and GPUs in the same rack/low-latency network — but often on-prem networks have more variability if shared with other workloads. direct connect to cloud regions adds 3-30ms typically but depends on link
[06:07] Lara: what about streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs at the protocol level — web sockets vs chunked transfer
[06:14] Priya: websockets reduce per-chunk HTTP overhead and are friendlier for real-time UI, but depending on proxy settings they can keep connections open and need careful resource management. chunked HTTP works too but has slightly higher per-chunk overhead. For p99 we look at open connection counts, proxy timeouts, and buffer flush behavior in the stack
[06:36] Alex: i'll throw in an example from a dedicated customer: they had p95 ~210ms p99 ~720ms on hosted because they were cross AZ; once they pinned to dedicated in single AZ and enabled sticky routing + q4_k_m config they got p95 ~150 p99 ~320ms
[06:55] Marco: interesting. are those numbers for streaming or non-streaming
[06:58] Alex: streaming
[07:00] Lara: ok can we talk about instrumentation — what do you need from our side to reproduce p99 spikes
[07:06] Priya: capture end-to-end traces: client timestamp at send, LB ingress timestamp, pod recv, server token timestamps, and response completion. also corpus of prompts and their token lengths so we can replay realistic load. a p95/p99 breakdown table per component helps
[07:24] Marco: we can share traffic captures, but they have PII — we'll scrub. also need to know if Redwood supports SAML SSO and SOC2 for sharing logs
[07:34] Alex: yes we have SOC2 and SSO info in the security pack — i'll share the security whitepaper and a redacted logging pipeline template
[07:42] Sofia: what about KMS for keying? we have strict KMS requirements
[07:46] Alex: we integrate with KMS/HSM and can support customer-managed keys in Private deployments
[07:52] Lara: any gotchas for heavy KV cache usage on private deployments
[07:56] Priya: main gotcha is cross-host cache hits — if you rely on a global cache with network attached storage, you add tail network latency. for Private we recommend local caches with warmup strategies, or colocated cache instances with fast network
[08:12] Marco: quantization question — do you support mixed precisions so we can run some models at q4 and some at fp16 on same cluster
[08:18] Priya: yes you can mix model variants; Redwood runtime can serve different quant profiles and we do smart routing to the matching instance. the scheduler avoids noisy neighbor effects by isolating heavy jobs
[08:30] Lara: what's the best way to run benchmarks with our traffic
[08:33] Priya: two steps: 1) replay your traffic profile against a test cluster with identical routing and network placement; 2) run synthetic token-level microbenchmarks to isolate runtime limits. we'll provide a benchmarking harness and scripts
[08:47] Alex: action item for us — we will run an initial benchmark on hosted with your scrubbed traces to get a baseline p95/p99 breakdown
[08:55] Lara: ok timeline?
[08:58] Alex: we can start next week if you share scrubbed traces by Friday
[09:02] Marco: what about cost implications of dedicated warm instances
[09:06] Alex: dedicated increases committed cost but reduces p99 spikes significantly for hot workloads. Redwood Optimize can model unit economics for both modes and estimate $/1M tokens
[09:18] Sofia: any competitors we should evaluate simultaneously
[09:21] Lara: we've looked at Anthropic, OpenAI managed endpoints, and some MSPs
[09:26] Priya: note on managed endpoints — some hide runtime-level telemetry which makes root cause hard. Redwood exposes token-level traces and sampling hooks
[09:38] Alex: ok last section - failure modes and graceful degradation. if model variant is busy we can fallback to smaller model with degradation policies and inform your app via headers so UX can adapt
[09:52] Marco: do you offer circuit breakers by call type
[09:55] Priya: yes you can set policy rules per route - rate limits, fallback thresholds, and canary percentages
[10:05] Lara: thanks this is great. let's recap next steps
